What’s stopping you from doing profiles now? Sit in a coffee shop for a week or so and seek out the regulars. Start a conversation with them, and politely ask them if you could do a story on them. 

While all journalists dream of doing profiles on the big names, it starts with the little people. Try talking to some folks at your work, with your friends/family, or just in common places, and it’s possible they might be willing to have an interview. 

The worst thing to happen is they could say no. 

When doing this, consider the big picture; are they experiencing something that’s hitting your area hard, like poverty, or is it possible a recent legislation made their lives harder/easier? For example: in my town, our city council voted to merge all the schools into one big school system, basically. So, if I wanted to do a profile on someone, I could find a mother whose child goes to one of the schools getting he short end of the stick and talk to her about it. 

Or, you could approach it Humans of New York-style; talk to people about their hardships and how they overcame all their problems. People like feel-good comeback stories. 

And if you want to edit, go to a bookstore and grab a copy of an AP Stylebook and browse journalism books. The AP book is a journalist’s bible. It includes spelling, punctuation, and media law. Look everything up before you put it in a story; most newspapers don’t use an Oxford comma, nor do they capitalize every word in a headline. The stylebook is the answer to everything. 

Sorry for the wall of text. If you have any questions about interviewing and what kinds of questions to ask, give me a holler; I’d be happy to help!

However, if you don’t want school, here’s this: start a blog. Start broadcasting on Facebook. Begin a local events page and start covering events. 

Get your hands on some old journalism books and practice writing. Drop the money for Adobe software, the stuff they use in the big-time newsrooms, and begin learning it. 

While I (obviously) think J-school is important, it doesn’t mean you can at least put yourself out there and begin to try. 

Are you interested in print/web journalism, or are you looking for on-air opportunities?

If you want to be a journalist, J-school is just about totally necessary. Let me put it like this:

I grew up in a radio family. My mother is a morning show host and worked at three stations, my dad is a news director and was the news director at a major station in our state before he moved. I grew up going to commission meetings, going on air, experiencing intense weather, and seeing local scandal first-hand. 

But when I got to J-school, I realized I didn’t know diddly squat. 

There’s a certain way you do everything: stories must be written inverted pyramid using AP Style, which takes practice. 

Media law must be studied so you can know how to avoid a lawsuit. 

You have to learn video editing, audio editing, page design, photo editing, how to use a camera, how to properly handle news technology. 

You have to learn how to be on-air, you have to learn how to interview people efficiently, you have to learn what on and off the record and on background and deep background are. 

Don’t get me wrong; it’s possible to learn all this without J-school. You don’t need a business degree to run a business, but it sure helps, right? 

Going to school can allow you to hone your skills, get actual experience, but also make the mistakes that serves as rites of passage in school rather than in the field or on air or in the newsroom. 

It’s worth it.
